doc.title: Al Gallodoro interviewed by Monk Rowe, Oneonta, New York, December 28, 2005

title: Recording the albums and the piece 'Idyell'
summary: Album session length, how Idyell grew from TV work, and the Henry Morgan spoofs.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: When you did an album in those days, how long did it take to do an album?

Well a session was three hours. But an album, no, that took more than three hours. It might have taken us all day. But it was “More Than You Can Stand.” It’s a long LP. That’s where I play “Saxophobia.” And then he wrote a piece called “Idyell” but it wasn’t called anything. I’ll tell you what happened. We used to do the Elgin Watch T.V. show and U.S. Steel Show. And in the studio Bernie had earphones on. And there’s a love scene going on in the movie. And a violin is playing this beautiful background music. So Bernie later got an idea to make it in a clarinet quintet. And he wrote the lead for me. It’s © Fillius Jazz Archive -14-
on that album “More Than You Can Stand,” called “Idyell.” Four clarinets and myself. It’s very beautiful. It only runs maybe two and a half or three minutes.
Did you used to do some kind of takeoffs on Wagner operas or something with him? On the Henry Morgan Show.
Yeah, yeah. That might be in “Mad.” And it might be in “More Than You Can Stand.”

Yeah. I’m pretty sure. One of those two. Henry Morgan was very funny, oh yeah. This Mad thing, the orchestra is fantastic. Absolutely fantastic. There again it’s all funny, but legitimate playing. Oh yes. All legitimate playing. Fast tonguing, fast this and that. And I think most of the time he used Ray Crisara. Ray is still alive as far as I know. He teaches in Austin, Texas, at the University of Austin. I did a concert there in 1990, June of — no, 1980.
